metaDescription: Six tower fans picked for bedrooms, compared on height, noise, timers, dimmable displays and sleep modes, with advice on aiming and placement.
expertTake: The Lasko 36 inch tower is the pick for a bedroom that wants a long-lived, simple fan with a timer, and the DREO 42 inch DC model is the pick for a taller bed and nine fine speeds. The Levoit adjustable tower is the choice for a high or low bed that needs the airflow aimed carefully. Anyone who shares a bed with a light sleeper should buy for the lowest setting, not the highest.
introParagraphs: A bedroom is the hardest place to use a fan. You need air moving across your body while you are barely conscious, with no noise, no glaring lights and no cold blast at the neck. The fan that cools a living room at full speed may be unbearable at 3 a.m.

That is why bedroom fans are judged on settings rather than ratings. Height decides whether the air reaches the pillow, the timer decides whether it runs all night, and the display and sleep mode decide whether you will want it near the bed at all.

products.name: Lasko 2510 36-Inch Oscillating Tower Fan with Remote and Timer
products.description:
The Lasko 2510 is a 36 inch tower with three whisper-quiet speeds, a 60 degree sweep and a remote that handles speed, oscillation and a timer. It is the plainest fan in this guide, and that is the reason it ranks first: fewer features mean fewer parts to rattle or fail across a decade of nights.

The 60 degree sweep covers a single bed or a pair of pillows rather than a whole room, which is exactly what a bedroom needs. The three speeds are well spaced, so the lowest is truly gentle and the highest cools a hot night. It lacks the DC motor and fine speed steps of the DREO models, so its motor is a little louder at any setting.

A long-established fan maker means replacement remotes and manuals are easy to find. Dust the grille monthly and keep the base level. As a gift, it works for anyone who dislikes electronics.
products.bestFor: A bedroom that needs a durable, simple fan with a timer.
pros: Timer and remote cover every function
60 degree sweep suits a single bed
cons: AC motor is louder than DC rivals
Narrow sweep will not cover a large room

products.name: DREO 42-Inch DC Tower Fan, 9 Speeds, 4 Modes, 90 Degree Sweep
products.description:
This DREO stands 42 inches tall, high enough to aim the airflow at a raised mattress or a sleeper's torso. A brushless DC motor is tuned for silence, and nine speeds with four modes let you pick the gentlest effective breeze.

Its 28 ft/s air speed is among the strongest in the bedroom group, though you will rarely run it near the top. The point is the low end: fine steps mean you can sit at a speed that is barely audible. A 90 degree sweep covers a queen bed and the room beside it. Against the Lasko it costs more and gives more control.

Height is a trade-off. A taller tower blows over a low bed, and it tips more easily on a soft carpet, so give it a firm base. Dust the grille monthly.
products.bestFor: A taller bed where fine speed control and a DC motor matter.
pros: 42 inch height reaches a raised mattress
Nine speeds with a silent DC motor
cons: Tall body tips more easily on soft carpet
Costs more than basic three-speed towers

products.name: Levoit 36 to 47 Inch Adjustable Tower Fan, 28 dB, Bladeless Style
products.description:
The Levoit is designed for high beds, with a height that adjusts from 36 to 47 inches and a lower section that can be taken off for a shorter fan. That flexibility matters in a bedroom because a bed can be anywhere from a low platform to a tall frame.

Its closed shell delivers 23 ft/s at about 28 dB, which is a gentle, quiet airflow rather than a strong one. A 90 degree sweep covers the bed and its surroundings. The closed shell has no exposed blades, which suits a child's room or a home with pets.

The adjustable section is the place to check for a wobble. Dust the intake monthly and wipe the shell. It is the pick when the height of the bed makes a fixed-height tower awkward.
products.bestFor: A very tall or very low bed where the fan height must be tuned.
pros: Closed shell with no exposed blades
Lower section removes for a shorter fan
cons: Adjustment joint can wobble if loose
Gentler airflow than the 28 ft/s towers

products.name: DREO 26 ft/s Tower Fan, 4 Speeds, 3 Modes, 8H Timer, 28 dB
products.description:
This DREO has an 8 hour timer that matches a night's sleep, four speeds and three modes, rated about 28 dB. The maker says the airflow reaches up to 33 feet, which is more than a bedroom needs, and the hypersilent tuning keeps the motor from adding hum.

Its simple controls are the appeal. Four speeds are enough for most sleepers, and the timer ends the airflow after you are asleep. It lacks the nine speed steps and the height of the 42 inch model, so the low end is a little less fine.

Vacuum the intake each month and keep the base flat. Sitting in the middle, it runs quieter than the Lasko and costs less than the 42 inch DREO.
products.bestFor: A sleeper who wants a night-length timer and quiet running.
pros: 8 hour timer fits a full night
26 ft/s airflow reaches across the room
cons: Fewer speed steps than the 9-speed model
Shorter body than the 42 inch tower

products.name: DREO TurboSilent Tower Fan, 26 ft/s, 5 Speeds, 4 Modes, Remote
products.description:
The TurboSilent tower runs near 28 dB with five speeds and four modes, and a remote lets you adjust it without leaving the bed. TurboSilent is the maker's name for the motor and airflow tuning that cuts noise.

It reaches 26 ft/s on its higher settings and offers a 90 degree sweep. The five speeds sit between the Lasko's three and the 42 inch DREO's nine, so it is a reasonable middle for fine control. The four modes include a natural-breeze setting that varies the speed.

Keep the grille clean and check remote batteries before hot nights. It is a safe, quiet choice for most bedrooms.
products.bestFor: A bedroom where a remote and several modes are valued.
cons: Less fine speed control than 9-speed fans
No stated sleep timer length in the listing data

products.name: PELONIS 30-Inch Oscillating Tower Fan, 3 Speeds, 7-Hour Timer
products.description:
The Pelonis is a short, 30 inch tower that fits on a nightstand or beside a low bed. It has a top control panel, a remote, three speeds and a 7 hour timer, and it assembles without tools.

Its short height means the airflow is low, so it works best for a low bed or for a person sitting up. A short fan also stands more stably. The CycleBoost label is the maker's name for its airflow design, and the simple controls keep it easy to use.

Dust the grille regularly and check the snap base. It is the right size for a small room or a child's bed.
products.bestFor: A small bedroom or a low bed where a short fan fits.

buyingCriteria.explanation: A fan only helps if the air reaches you. A 30 inch tower such as the Pelonis suits a low bed or a nightstand, a 36 inch Lasko suits a standard bed, and a 42 inch DREO or an adjustable Levoit suits a raised mattress. Measure from the floor to the top of your mattress before you buy, and aim the airflow at your torso rather than your face. A fan that blows over the top of a low bed does nothing for the sleeper and simply stirs the ceiling, while one aimed at the face dries the eyes and throat and wakes people with a stiff neck. Many sleepers prefer to aim the fan at the foot of the bed, where the moving air cools the legs and the covers without a draught on the head.

Bedroom fans are used at their lowest settings, so the quoted noise at low speed is the one that counts. The DREO and Levoit towers claim about 28 dB, which is close to a quiet whisper. A fan that is quiet only at its lowest setting but too weak to be useful there defeats the purpose, so check that the lowest speed still moves air. It is worth reading the lowest setting as a number as well as a rating: on a three-speed fan the bottom step can be fairly strong, while on a nine-step fan it is truly gentle. That difference is the best argument for paying more for a DC motor, because the quietest useful speed is where you will spend nearly every night.

A timer lets the fan run while you fall asleep and then stop, which saves power and avoids the chill of a fan running all night. The DREO 26 ft/s tower offers 8 hours, the Pelonis 7, and the Lasko has a timer with a remote. Match the timer to your habit: all night, or just the first hour. People who wake when the fan stops should skip the timer and use a low steady speed, and people who wake from the chill should use the shortest timer that gets them into deep sleep. A timer also trims the power bill slightly, though a modern DC fan draws so little that the saving is a matter of cents, not dollars.

A bright LED panel in a dark bedroom is a nuisance. Look for a display that dims or turns off, or a sleep mode that does it automatically. If the fan lacks one, a small piece of tape over the LED is a free fix, though it will not help a fan whose buttons are lit as well.

A 60 degree sweep like the Lasko covers a single bed. A 90 degree sweep, as on the DREO and Levoit, covers a double bed and the space around it. A wider sweep dilutes the breeze at any one place, so choose the narrowest arc that covers the bed. Some people prefer a fixed fan aimed at their feet. Couples often disagree about airflow, and an oscillating fan that sweeps across both pillows at a low speed is a common compromise. If one partner is always cold, keep the fan pointed at the other side of the bed and let the sweep angle settle the argument rather than the speed dial.

A tall fan is top-heavy, and a child or a pet can knock it over. A closed shell like the Levoit avoids exposed blades, while a conventional tower has a grille. Place the fan on a hard, level floor away from curtains, and keep the cord out of walkways. A bedroom fan also sits where someone walks half-asleep to the bathroom, so choose a spot that is not on the path, and consider a cord clip along the baseboard. If a child or a large pet shares the room, test the fan by giving it a firm nudge: a base that tips on a gentle push is the wrong fan for that room.

howWeEvaluated.title: Quiet at low speeds
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared noise ratings and motor types, since bedroom use is at the low end. DC-motor models at about 28 dB lead.

howWeEvaluated.title: Height and aim
howWeEvaluated.description: We matched fan heights to bed heights. The adjustable Levoit and 42 inch DREO suit tall beds, and the Pelonis suits low ones.

howWeEvaluated.title: Night features
howWeEvaluated.description: We counted timers, sleep modes and dimmable displays. The DREO 8 hour timer and Lasko timer remote score well.

howWeEvaluated.title: Simplicity and durability
howWeEvaluated.description: We favoured simple designs with fewer parts. The Lasko leads here.

howWeEvaluated.title: Safety
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered stability and shell design. The closed Levoit shell suits homes with children and pets.

cards.label: Timer
cards.text: A timer, such as the DREO 8 hour or Pelonis 7 hour, stops the fan after a set period. It suits people who want to fall asleep cool and wake without a draught.

cards.label: Sleep mode
cards.text: A sleep mode, as on the 42 inch DREO, steps the fan down over the night. It suits people who want continuous gentle airflow that gets quieter as the room cools.

howToChoose.note: Choose a timer for simplicity and a sleep mode for comfort across the whole night.

rows: Nine steps and a silent DC motor
Gentle low speed and a timer

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Look for quiet at low speed, a timer, a dimmable or off display and a height that matches the bed. Aim the airflow at your torso, not your face, and use the lowest speed that keeps you comfortable.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The 42 inch DREO is the most refined, the Lasko 2510 is the simplest, and the Levoit adjustable is the best for unusual bed heights.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Spend more if you are a light sleeper or run the fan every night. The 42 inch DREO and Levoit adjustable pay back in quiet and fit.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Save if the fan runs a few hot weeks a year. The Pelonis or Lasko moves plenty of air.

maintenance.why: Bedrooms collect lint from bedding that clogs fans. A soft brush clears it.
Dust builds near the outlet and raises noise.
A loose base rattles and tips. Tighten the screws and place the fan on a firm floor.
A dead remote forces you out of bed. Keep spares in a drawer.
A cover keeps dust out of the intake and off the grille over winter.

faq.q: How close should a tower fan be to the bed?
faq.a: A few feet is enough for a quiet fan. Aim it across your body rather than at your face, and use the lowest speed that keeps you cool.

faq.q: Is it safe to leave a fan on all night?
faq.a: A modern tower fan is designed for continuous use. Keep the grille clear, the base stable and the cord out of the way, and avoid placing it where bedding can block the intake.

faq.q: Which is quieter, a tower or a desk fan?
faq.a: A desk fan can be quieter at arm's length, because it runs at a low airspeed. A tower covers more of the bed, so choose by distance to the pillow.

faq.q: Do fans help with white noise?
faq.a: Many people sleep better with a steady, low sound. A fan on its lowest speed can serve, but the sound should be smooth, not pulsing or rattling.

faq.q: Will a fan cool the room?
faq.a: No, it moves air across your skin and feels cooler. In an empty room it does nothing, so turn it off when you leave.

faq.q: Why is my fan louder over time?
faq.a: Dust on the impeller and a loose base are the usual causes. Clean the intake and check the base before blaming the motor.
